Microsoft is seeking to secure adequate power supplies for its data centers without relying on government subsidies or imposing additional burdens on other electricity consumers. Zhitong Finance APP reports: $Microsoft (MSFT.US)$ The company is seeking to ensure adequate power supply for its data centers without relying on government subsidies or increasing the burden on other electricity consumers. As artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure continues to expand, the substantial energy demands of data centers have become an increasingly prominent issue in U.S. social and political discourse. Noelle Walsh, President of Cloud Operations and Innovation at Microsoft, stated at a conference in Houston: "We do not want other consumers to foot the bill for our growth. We will bear the costs ourselves." Microsoft plans to invest $117 billion this year in computing infrastructure for AI and cloud computing services. As tech giants continue to expand their data center footprint, issues such as tight power supply, high grid construction costs, and rising residential electricity bills are sparking growing controversy. Data center construction has even become one of the key issues in this month's U.S. midterm elections. The election results, which saw Democrats gain control of Congress, reflect increasing political attention on energy costs and the impact of large-scale technology projects on local communities. As a long-term supporter of OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, Microsoft has consistently emphasized that its data center construction adheres to a "community-first" principle. This means that related projects should deliver tangible benefits to local residents, rather than imposing the negative consequences of rising electricity costs and infrastructure expansion on local communities. In this context, Microsoft is collaborating with energy giant $Chevron (CVX.US)$ and investment firm Engine No. 1 to develop a large-scale data center and power infrastructure project in West Texas, named Project Kilby. The project adopts an independent power supply model, involving the construction of dedicated power generation facilities near the data center to supply electricity directly, thereby reducing reliance on the public grid. This approach is expected to help large technology companies meet growing computing demand while minimizing the impact of data center expansion on other electricity users. However, Project Kilby currently faces regulatory hurdles. Previously, Texas Governor Greg Abbott suspended approvals for new data center projects, hindering the progress of this development plan. In the recent gubernatorial election, Abbott lost to Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa. Notably, Hinojosa indicated during her campaign that she might adopt a stricter stance on approving data center projects. This suggests that, despite the change in state leadership, relevant projects may still face significant policy uncertainty. Nevertheless, Chevron still plans to proceed with the construction of Project Kilby according to the established schedule, aiming for initial operations by 2028 and full commercial operation by 2031. Jeff Gustavson, President of Chevron New Energies, stated that any project failing to generate net benefits for the local community is ultimately destined to struggle. He emphasized that Project Kilby is expected to create jobs in West Texas and provide stable tax revenue for local governments, thereby ensuring that data center construction not only serves the computing power needs of technology companies but also creates long-term economic value for the host communities. As investment in U.S. AI infrastructure continues to expand, how technology companies address power supply issues has become a key factor influencing the successful implementation of data center projects. Microsoft’s commitment to bear its own energy costs and avoid passing additional burdens onto other consumers highlights that large tech companies are attempting to alleviate the energy and regulatory pressures triggered by the AI construction boom by building their own supporting power facilities and strengthening community cooperation. title: NYU Stern Launches AI Startup Competition With $5 Million Gift From Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Executive Jeff Teper And Wife Sandy - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 11, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Each spring, cohorts of NYU Stern students will compete to build AI-native business solutions, with annual prize pools exceeding $100,000 up for grabs. The competition, called The Teper Innovation Challenge, will feature distinct tracks for both undergraduate and MBA students, with the first round scheduled to begin in the spring 2027 semester. Behind the initiative are Stern alumni Jeff Teper (NASDAQ: MSFT), Executive Vice President for Apps and Agents at Microsoft, and his wife Alexandra “Sandy” Teper, who together donated $5 million to their alma mater. Jeff graduated from Stern in 1986, while Sandy earned her degree a year earlier in 1985, and the two met as students at the Greenwich Village school before building parallel careers in technology. At Microsoft, Jeff is credited with scaling SharePoint from its early days into a billion-dollar enterprise product and has since guided teams through successive waves of cloud computing and artificial intelligence adoption. The $5 million commitment goes beyond the competition itself, with a portion earmarked to expand student access to frontier technology tools and support the deeper integration of advanced AI into Stern’s broader academic curriculum. NYU Stern Dean Bharat Anand credited the couple’s long-standing connection to the school, saying they have “always made time for Stern” even while breaking new ground in technology and business throughout their careers. Anand added that “advances in AI are making it easier than ever for anyone to turn ideas into something tangible,” framing the challenge as an extension of the experiential learning philosophy central to Stern’s identity. In a joint statement, Sandy and Jeff pointed to the scale of the current moment, noting: “Now with the even larger artificial intelligence transformation, we are thrilled to support Stern students as they explore, collaborate, and create opportunities in this next wave of technology and the economy.” Jeff’s relationship with Stern predates this gift by several years, having joined the school’s Tech Board as part of its inaugural cohort of industry leaders, a body established alongside the launch of the Andre Koo Tech MBA program. He has also hosted Stern students at Microsoft’s Seattle campus, sponsored experiential learning projects in New York City, and advised faculty who developed what the school describes as one of the first agentic AI courses offered at a major business school. The Teper Innovation Challenge is set to formally launch in the coming weeks, positioning Stern to compete for recognition as a leading incubator of AI-literate business talent ahead of a crowded field of peer institutions. title: February 2027 Microsoft Entra MFA Deadline Pushes Soprano Design (MSFT +2.74%) To Launch SMS And Voice Authentication Bridge - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 11, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A hard deadline is concentrating minds across enterprise IT departments, with Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) set to retire SMS and Voice delivery inside Microsoft Entra ID from February 1, 2027. The move is part of a broader shift by the technology giant toward passkeys as its preferred default authentication experience for users. Organisations that still depend on telephony-based multi-factor authentication will be required to source and manage their own third-party providers once Microsoft withdraws the built-in capability. Sydney-based Soprano Design, which powers more than 32 billion secure interactions annually across 4,500-plus organisations, has stepped into that gap with a dedicated integration product. The company has launched Soprano Connect for Microsoft Entra, making it available through the Microsoft Security Store under both per-user and per-transaction pricing structures. Soprano has held Microsoft partner status for more than 15 years, giving it an established position from which to serve enterprise and government clients affected by the upcoming retirement. Chief Technology Officer Mohamed Odah framed the challenge as one of balancing progress with operational continuity, saying: “Having provided secure authentication solutions to our enterprise and government customers for more than 30 years, we understand that organisations must balance the adoption of new authentication methods with continuity for the users, systems and requirements they support today.” Director of Product and Development Asha Potla cautioned against underestimating the complexity involved, noting that “for many organisations, this won’t be a simple switch from one authentication method to another.” Potla added that varying regulatory requirements, user groups, and system dependencies can create sharply different authentication needs even within a single organisation, and that early planning is critical. Microsoft’s own partner product manager for security, Ankur Patel, endorsed the integration’s rationale directly, stating: “Security continuity is key to our ecosystem. As we evolve our authentication practices, we want customers to have clear options that meet their business needs.” Patel went further, noting that Soprano’s connection to Microsoft Entra ID workforce tenants gives clients “the flexibility to choose the telephony provider that best supports their users and organizational requirements.” The product is specifically targeted at businesses with regulatory, technical, or operational mandates that prevent a clean migration away from SMS or Voice MFA before the retirement rollout begins. Soprano Design operates globally from its Sydney headquarters and serves clients across healthcare, finance, logistics, and government sectors, markets where authentication continuity carries significant compliance weight. title: What Has Changed About Owning Microsoft Stock? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. If you own Microsoft (MSFT), you probably bought it as a company that turns much of what it sells into spare cash for dividends and buybacks. Its fiscal first-quarter report on October 28, 2026, is a fair moment to check that picture, because management said on that call it will access additional sources of funding when it believes doing so is attractive. So what has actually shifted inside the business you own? Microsoft Now Reinvests Far More Of Each Sales Dollar Over the twelve months to September 2026, Microsoft’s capital spending reached 39.2% of its revenue. That figure compares with a median of 10.7% over the 52 quarter ends from December 2012 to September 2025. This heavier spending leaves the company with less surplus cash. Free cash flow, the cash Microsoft retains after that spending, accounted for 17.3% of revenue over the same twelve months, compared with a median of 29.5% in those earlier years. The latest quarter reflects the same shift. During fiscal Q1 2027, free cash flow fell to $18.6 billion from $25.7 billion a year earlier, even though revenue grew. Microsoft is not generating less cash, since cash from operations kept rising over the twelve months. The company is funneling far more of that cash back into the business. According to management on the October 28 call, Microsoft is spending more because demand for its cloud capacity is running ahead of what the company has. Executives said that accelerating demand led the company to add 24 new data centers in the quarter, and that customer demand continues to exceed available supply. This demand is visible within the cloud business itself. Revenue from Azure, Microsoft’s cloud platform, increased 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, a pace management said was ahead of expectations. Microsoft still funds its dividends and buybacks out of free cash flow, but the company operates with far less to spare. Over the twelve months to September 2026, Microsoft paid $48.0 billion in dividends and buybacks out of $60.0 billion of free cash flow. A year earlier, it paid $44.7 billion out of $78.0 billion. The company’s cash pile has shrunk as well. Cash and short-term investments fell to $64.3 billion at the end of September 2026, down from $102 billion a year earlier. This total remains higher than Microsoft’s $57.2 billion of debt, so the company continues to hold net cash. Here is news a holder can like: debt was 7.3% of Microsoft’s assets at the end of September 2026, against a median of 19.0% from December 2012 to September 2025. With so little debt, Microsoft has room to borrow, and after the call it expected to raise $25 billion in a U.S. bond sale. Management expects the spending to keep rising, to over $50 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, against $45.2 billion in the first quarter. That $45.2 billion counts finance leases when they begin; the cash Microsoft paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion. Historically, a Microsoft shareholder could assume a large share of every sales dollar would return as spare cash, leaving plenty left over after the dividend and the buyback. That dynamic no longer holds. The spending pays off for investors only if Microsoft turns its new capacity into revenue, and management said each dollar of capital spending has the potential to support more revenue and higher returns over time. When the company reports again, expected in January 2027, the figures to watch will be Microsoft’s capital spending against its revenue and the free cash flow left after it. title: Microsoft MSFT Stock Drops From the Highs on Excel Challenge Following Anthropic Workplace Software Announcement - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock retreated from a record high near $560 after Anthropic unveiled new workplace software, intensifying competition for Microsoft 365 while investors continue to assess infrastructure spending, future computing commitments and the profitability of cloud expansion. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares rallied sharply last week, recovering from a decline toward $500 to approach $560 and establish a new record high. Improving sentiment across technology stocks following the U.S. midterm elections helped attract buyers, despite growing concerns about data-centre spending, financing requirements and the returns on massive computing investments. However, the recovery has lost momentum this week. Microsoft shares dropped more than 3% to $530.39 following Anthropic’s announcement of new workplace software, raising concerns about competition in one of Microsoft’s most important business segments. Anthropic introduced a suite of workplace tools, including a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, its spreadsheet service targeting the market dominated by Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. Several products are reportedly available in beta to paying users. The company also plans to allow enterprises to embed existing applications into Claude, potentially turning the platform into a central interface for workplace tasks rather than simply an assistant that helps users operate software. For Microsoft, this represents a competitive challenge beyond the traditional software market. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in revenue during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, ended September 30, 2026, increasing approximately 17% year-over-year and accounting for roughly 30% of total revenue. Although this figure includes commercial and consumer cloud businesses rather than Excel alone, it illustrates the importance of Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results demonstrated substantial earnings growth, with net income increasing 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, comfortably exceeding expectations, while earnings surpassed the analyst consensus of $4.27 per share. Microsoft Cloud revenue also delivered strong growth, reaching $63.9 billion, up 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, strong earnings have not eliminated questions about infrastructure spending. Data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require substantial capital investment. Investors increasingly want evidence that cloud revenue can grow quickly enough to justify these commitments without weakening margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments to Microsoft through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. The arrangement highlights the scale of future computing demand but also raises questions about the financial commitments required to support expanding infrastructure capacity. Microsoft has a stronger balance sheet than smaller cloud providers, but elevated borrowing costs and uncertain customer spending could create problems across the sector. Concerns about debt-funded data-centre construction have intensified as investors reassess whether projected demand will justify the cost of expansion. Microsoft is also developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce dependence on external chip suppliers. The custom processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver substantially higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually lower computing costs and improve infrastructure economics. However, development and deployment require significant investment before those efficiency gains translate into stronger profitability. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the status of those discussions remains unclear. Microsoft’s consumer businesses present a less encouraging picture. The Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year-over-year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. Regulatory scrutiny is another potential challenge. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing oversight of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace and Anthropic’s expanding workplace software offering could further pressure Microsoft’s subscription business as enterprises reassess costs and alternatives. For investors, the latest reversal from $560 highlights a changing market narrative. Microsoft continues to deliver strong earnings and cloud growth, but competition, infrastructure commitments and the cost of expanding computing capacity are becoming increasingly important. The next challenge is demonstrating that its enormous investments can generate sustainable returns rather than simply supporting an increasingly expensive expansion cycle.

Microsoft (MSFT) is getting paid for artificial intelligence (AI) agents, software that can finish tasks on its own. The maker of Windows and Microsoft 365 now charges more and more customers for how much work these agents do. This makes me bullish on Microsoft. Its AI push is starting to pay for itself, and the company keeps very high margins even while it spends heavily on data centers. The latest quarter backs that up. Revenue from Azure, Microsoft's cloud platform, grew 48%. The operating margin, the share of sales left after operating costs, reached about 50%. The stock is up 9.7% this year. It is no longer cheap after its rally since June, and AI spending keeps climbing. However, I believe agents give Microsoft a clear way to earn that money back. Microsoft gets paid for AI agents mostly through usage. Copilot, its AI assistant, has mainly been sold as a monthly per-user license, but customers can now also buy credits and pay for the work their agents do. Copilot customers using these credits grew more than 75% in a single quarter, while paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats rose just 5% year-over-year. Get 75% Off TipRanks Premium and unlock powerful investing tools to make smarter, more confident investment decisions Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks The two figures measure different things, but the difference in pace stands out. License sales follow a customer's headcount, while credit sales follow the work agents take on, which can grow much faster. Agent 365, Microsoft's registry for managing a company's agents, now holds more than 50 million agents, up over 30% in one quarter. Foundry, where companies build their own AI apps and agents, passed 120,000 customers, and its revenue more than tripled year-over-year. I think Copilot is a big part of Microsoft's future, because usage keeps climbing. Daily users grew more than fivefold year-over-year, and user satisfaction is at an all-time high. Big companies are buying in, too. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold in a year, and Volkswagen (VWAGY) has rolled out Copilot to more than 330,000 employees. For Microsoft, more usage now means more revenue. Azure keeps speeding up, and agents are part of the reason, since they need a lot of computing power. Its revenue grew 48% in the September quarter, ahead of what Wall Street expected, helped by Foundry. Management expects 49% to 50% growth in the December quarter, excluding currency effects. Microsoft is also getting more out of its hardware. Copilot workload throughput, meaning how much AI work its systems can process, rose more than 50% in one quarter, which should make each AI task cheaper to run. Microsoft's AI spending is high, but I think it is manageable. The company spent $135.9 billion on capex over the past four quarters, mostly on data centers and chips, and that number is still rising. The risk of overinvesting will always be there. That is why return on invested capital (ROIC) is the number I watch most closely. It shows how much profit a company makes on the money put into its business. Adding up the last four quarters gives Microsoft an ROIC of about 22%, so it earns roughly 22 cents on every dollar invested. That is slightly lower than a year earlier, but returns have improved in each of the last two quarters, so I don't see a red flag during such a big build-out. Microsoft is also careful with cash. Over the past 12 months, it still had about $60 billion of free cash flow, the money left after capex. I usually prefer companies that spend more aggressively, but I understand why Microsoft doesn't want to make its shareholders nervous. In late October, it raised $25 billion in its first major U.S. bond sale since 2017, which gives it more room to keep building data centers without draining its own cash. Management expects free cash flow to stay positive in Fiscal 2027 and says it is confident these investments will pay off over the long run. That convinces me, because agents are already turning part of this spending into revenue. Microsoft stock isn't too expensive, in my view, although it is no longer cheap. Its trailing-12-month (TTM) price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is around 27.7x, based on reported profit, so investors pay about $27.7 for each dollar Microsoft earns in a year. That is higher than the 20.72x it traded at when Fiscal 2026 ended in June, after a sharp sell-off in the first half of the year. Still, it is well below the levels of the three fiscal years before that, when the P/E ended each year above 35x. Looking at the next 12 months, the forward P/E is about 26x, based on analysts' estimates of adjusted earnings, which leave out the impact of Microsoft's investment in OpenAI. I think 26x is a fair price for a company that keeps about half of its sales as operating profit. The main risk is margins. Microsoft's cloud gross margin, the share of cloud revenue left after the direct cost of running it, is already shrinking as lower-margin Azure makes up a bigger part of cloud sales. Management also expects operating margin to dip slightly from a year earlier in the December quarter. If that continues, the stock will start to look expensive. Wall Street sees Microsoft very positively, with a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 35 Buys, four Holds, and zero Sells assigned in the last three months. At $632.48, the average Microsoft price target implies 16.01% upside potential. Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler, one of the top analysts on TipRanks, raised his price target to $722 from $662 after the September-quarter report and reiterated his Outperform (Buy) rating on November 6, implying about 32% upside. He believes lower-than-expected capex and capacity delays created some unwarranted noise around solid results, and I fully agree. I'm bullish on Microsoft. It is spending a lot on AI, and I can already see how that money comes back through agents that customers pay for as they use them. The next test is keeping returns this high while the build-out continues. So far, Microsoft is passing it. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

title: Microsoft’s Neocloud Pullback Isn’t a Crack in AI Demand - MarketBeat
content:
On Nov. 5, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft Corp. NASDAQ: MSFT is stepping away from risky projects with Nebius NASDAQ: NBIS, IREN NASDAQ: IREN and Nscale and debating new neocloud deals. The Financial Times added that Microsoft passed on an option to more than double its Nscale contract in Texas. Those reports, coming on the heels of the U.S. midterm elections, sent neocloud stocks tumbling.  By the end of the day, NBIS was down about 14%, IREN dropped 17%, and CoreWeave NASDAQ: CRWV dropped 10%. Many investors interpreted the news as the first crack in AI demand. The fundamentals tell a different story. Days earlier, Microsoft reported 48% Azure growth and said demand still exceeds supply. Some investors pointed out a less-than-expected capital expenditure (CapEx) number. However, that fell short because third-party suppliers delivered late, not because Microsoft spent less by choice. That context reframes the neocloud news. Bloomberg cited a $1 million fine for unpermitted generators at a New Jersey site being built for Nebius. It also flagged cabling problems at an IREN site in Texas. Microsoft is demanding better execution and building more of its own capacity. Microsoft’s recent moves share a common thread. Each one targets a specific supplier problem. None of them points to weaker demand. For example, a source familiar with the Nscale decision told Reuters that Microsoft made that decision several months ago. The existing Texas contract remains in place. Microsoft declined an expansion option, but it didn't cancel live capacity. The same pattern shows up elsewhere. Microsoft exited an Nscale project in England after grid delays pushed power into the 2030s. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft is winding down a 2023 Oracle deal. The reason given was older NVIDIA chips that no longer meet Microsoft’s specifications. Both of those examples provide nuance to the delays with IREN. On its earnings call, the company communicated that Microsoft requested network design changes that pushed some deliveries into early 2027. The company said it faces no financial penalties for those changes, and that its vertically integrated business model put it in a position to manage the changes in ways that other neoclouds would not be able to do. The numbers from Microsoft’s fiscal first quarter support that reading. Azure revenue grew 48% to $33.2 billion, surpassing management’s guidance of 44% to 45%. Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate to 49% to 50% in the current quarter. Microsoft’s commercial backlog tells a similar story. Remaining performance obligations rose 73% to $677 billion. That represents contracted future revenue that Microsoft has yet to recognize. A company with that backlog cannot afford unreliable suppliers. Investors have seen this movie before. In early 2025, reports that Microsoft was canceling data center leases sparked fears of an AI slowdown. Microsoft’s capital spending kept climbing anyway. There is a tradeoff investors should not ignore. Renting capacity from neoclouds spreads costs over the life of a contract. Building it means paying more up front. If Microsoft owns more capacity, more of the cost lands on its own balance sheet. That cost is already visible. Free cash flow fell about 27% to $18.6 billion last quarter. Operating cash flow rose 29% to $58 billion over the same period. The gap reflects how much cash Microsoft is pouring into data centers. Spending is set to rise from here. CFO Amy Hood guided for CapEx above $50 billion in the December quarter. She also expects spending to accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year. That includes third-party capacity that slipped from earlier quarters. The mix of that spending matters too. Hood said roughly 75% of CapEx now goes to short-lived assets such as GPUs and CPUs. Those chips lose value far faster than buildings do. Owning more of them puts more pressure on future margins. Investors should ask whether “build, don’t rent” means even heavier CapEx ahead. Microsoft hasn’t said how much neocloud capacity it plans to replace with its own. That answer will shape free cash flow for years. For neocloud stocks, the sell-off may not be pure overreaction. Microsoft is a major customer for Nebius, IREN, and Nscale. If it concentrates on fewer suppliers, the risk to those business models is real. Execution now matters as much as headline contract values. IREN’s backlog grew 22% to $20.3 billion last quarter. But the company still needs about $6 billion in financing for its fiscal 2027 spending plan. Delivery delays make that harder. For MSFT shareholders, the picture is more favorable. Demand remains ahead of supply, and Microsoft is using its leverage to secure better capacity. The open question is cost, not demand. Key dates will test the thesis. Nebius reports earnings on Nov. 12. IREN is targeting January 2027 to bring more than $4 billion in contracted annual recurring revenue online, although additional supplier delays could push that milestone into February. content: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) shares surged 2.34% to $543.03 on Monday, gaining $12.42 amid strong buying momentum. The stock approached an intraday high near $546. Meanwhile, Northern Trust announced an expanded Microsoft partnership focused on institutional client onboarding. Northern Trust introduced an AI-powered onboarding agent for its Front Office Solutions platform. The companies developed the system through their engineering teams to simplify complex investment data processing. The project extends their collaboration into asset servicing operations. Front Office Solutions supports foundations, pension funds, endowments, and large family offices. These clients often maintain transaction records across systems. Consequently, onboarding teams must organize historical data before the platform can generate consistent performance reports. Alternative investments add complexity because their records require reconstruction. Northern Trust’s survey found that 57% of asset owners identified fragmented data consolidation as their leading challenge. The new agent addresses that problem by converting client transaction histories into a standard reporting format. Northern Trust reported that the agent reduced data preparation time from two and a half weeks to three days. That change represents an 83% reduction in the measured process. The company also reported a 96.5% first-pass F1 score for the system’s output. The F1 measure combines precision and recall to assess the quality of automated results. However, Northern Trust analysts still review the agent’s decisions and correct exceptions. This process helps teams identify errors before clients begin using the reporting platform. The system operates on Microsoft Azure and uses Microsoft Foundry. It also connects with Excel and SharePoint, providing tools for approval. Meanwhile, a governed knowledge layer retains approved onboarding information to support future work. Microsoft and Northern Trust designed the system around financial services privacy and governance requirements. Microsoft evaluated performance with anonymized data while Northern Trust retained control of client information. This approach allowed the engineering teams to improve results without exposing clients’ underlying records. The firms also built human oversight into the workflow rather than removing analysts from decisions. Northern Trust expects automation to reduce repetitive preparation work and create more time for specialized tasks. Its strategy combines automated processing with staff judgment across sensitive client operations. The announcement illustrates Microsoft’s push to apply enterprise AI within heavily regulated financial institutions. For Northern Trust, the rollout targets an operational bottleneck that affects onboarding speed and reporting readiness. title: Microsoft (MSFT.US) Reportedly Plans to Reduce Reliance on Neoclouds Amid Resistance to AI Infrastructure Expansion - 富途牛牛
content: According to CNBC, citing people familiar with the matter, Microsoft (MSFT.US) is reducing its neocloud partner list, focusing on collaboration with a select few major vendors, and expanding its own data centers. The plan poses another potential challenge for certain segments of the artificial intelligence market. With borrowing costs rising, heavy debt burdens, and market concerns that the pace of infrastructure expansion may slow, related industries are already showing signs of strain. In recent years, Microsoft has established cooperative relationships with several neocloud companies, including CoreWeave (CRWV.US), Nebius (NBIS.US), Chronoscale (CHRN.US), IREN (IREN.US), Lambda, Nscale, and Oracle (ORCL.US), which is making substantial investments in AI infrastructure. Two sources said Microsoft is still in the evaluation phase and has not yet decided which neoclouds to discontinue. One of them noted that Microsoft aims to prioritize expanding its own data center infrastructure. Bloomberg had earlier reported on these plans. Additionally, two other sources stated that Microsoft has chosen not to renew its cooperation agreement with Oracle. A Microsoft spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its infrastructure strategy "is built on flexibility and choice." The spokesperson said, "We combine Microsoft's own data centers, leased facilities, and strategic partnerships with third-party vendors to provide the required capacity where and when our customers need it. We regularly review these investments in line with customer demand, including tracking delivery progress and adjusting plans as circumstances change." In recent weeks, neocloud-related stocks have been volatile on Wall Street. Rising interest rates have heightened market concerns about companies' rapid capacity expansion and over-reliance on debt. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN have all fallen by about half over the past month, even after a rebound last Friday (the 6th). A recent industry study found that there are currently 323 neocloud companies, and experts predict that many of them will struggle to survive. IREN said when it announced its results last Thursday that it had delivered data center capacity to Microsoft in August, but Microsoft requested an upgrade of network equipment, causing the related infrastructure to be commissioned in January or February next year instead of within this year. During the company's fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings call in October, Microsoft CFO Amy Hood stated that some cloud contracts involving graphics processors have been delayed until the first half of 2027, impacting the growth of Azure's cloud business. Microsoft's latest quarterly capital expenditures and finance leases totaled $45.2 billion, and the company indicated that capital spending will accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year. CoreWeave and Nebius are set to release their quarterly results. IREN's shares surged 16% last Friday after the company reported that AI revenue more than doubled quarter-over-quarter to $200 million. IREN Co-CEO Daniel Roberts told CNBC, "There is a disconnect between what we see in the public markets and at the client level." However, he acknowledged that the market environment poses challenges. Roberts said on the earnings call, "Capital markets have become more selective over the past few weeks, and market focus has undoubtedly shifted from contract size to delivery capability, financing, and profitability." Microsoft had earlier scaled back its partnership with the UK's neocloud Nscale, abandoning a planned site in England. In October, Darren Hardman, Microsoft's president for the UK and Ireland, told CNBC that the decision was related to Nscale's ability to secure power supply. The Financial Times reported this week that Microsoft has decided not to renew Nscale's contract in Texas. Nscale filed for an IPO in mid-September but has not updated its prospectus since. In its IPO filing, the company stated that it expected Microsoft to become a "significant customer" in the future. Microsoft's major shift to CoreWeave began after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, when demand for GPUs surged. In search of alternative supply sources, Microsoft partnered with CoreWeave, which was still privately held at the time and originated from cryptocurrency mining operations. When CoreWeave went public last year, it stated that 62% of its 2024 revenue would come from Microsoft. When ChatGPT launched, OpenAI used only Azure. Its current cloud providers also include Amazon (AMZN.US), Cerebras (CBRS.US), CoreWeave, Google, and Oracle. A Microsoft spokesperson said that reviewing the neocloud investment is a "normal and responsible way to manage large, complex infrastructure projects," adding that "the pace of the new agreement reflects current actual needs."
